scenarios.title: Where to Start in Python
scenarios.situation: You're an Excel power user — VLOOKUP, pivot tables, charts — with zero Python. Your manager wants the weekly report automated, and 'learn ML' is on your growth plan.
scenarios.prompt: What is the fastest on-ramp into Python for ML?
evidence: your skills
Pivot tables, INDEX/MATCH, filtering, charting — deep tabular intuition.
the goal
Automate the weekly report first; ML comes second.
choices: Learn pandas first — DataFrames mirror the spreadsheet mental model: filter, groupby, and pivot_table map directly to what you already know.
Start with Python classes and object-oriented theory to build a proper foundation.
Learn NumPy linear algebra first — ML is math, so start with math.
Skip Python and keep everything in Excel — the report works fine as it is.
scenarios.why: pandas is the translation layer: filtering is WHERE, groupby is GROUP BY, merge is JOIN, pivot_table is the pivot table. Learning the mapping (not a new worldview) gets you automating the real report within days, which builds the momentum and the data intuition that ML later requires.
scenarios.hint: Which Python tool looks most like a spreadsheet?

scenarios.title: The 40-Minute Loop
scenarios.situation: Your script loops over 2 million rows with df.iterrows(), doing simple arithmetic per row. It takes over 40 minutes, and the report is due hourly.
scenarios.prompt: How do you fix the performance?
evidence: the code
for i, row in df.iterrows(): ... — Python-level loop over 2M rows.
the operation
Simple arithmetic per row — no complex logic.
choices: Vectorize: express the arithmetic as whole-column operations — pandas/NumPy run it in C, 10–100x faster.
Buy a bigger machine with more cores.
Split the data into 10 chunks and run the same loop on each.
Rewrite the loop with a second thread.
scenarios.why: iterrows() pays Python interpreter overhead per row; vectorized column ops push the loop into compiled C code. For simple arithmetic the speedup is typically 10–100x — no new hardware needed. (Threads don't help either: the GIL keeps Python-level loops serial.)
scenarios.hint: Can the operation be written without mentioning rows at all?

scenarios.title: First Churn Model
scenarios.situation: You've been asked to predict customer churn (yes/no) from clean tabular data: 50k rows, 20 features. Marketing wants to understand the drivers, not just get scores.
scenarios.prompt: Which first model do you build?
evidence: the data
50k rows, 20 features, binary label — plenty for simple models.
the need
Marketing must understand WHY customers churn, to act on it.
choices: Logistic regression — an interpretable baseline whose coefficients marketing can read as drivers.
A 200-layer neural network — maximum capacity for the patterns.
K-means clustering — group customers and guess which cluster churns.
A hand-written rules list with 300 branches — fully transparent.
scenarios.why: The first model should be a baseline you can explain: logistic regression gives calibrated probabilities and readable coefficients (each feature's directional effect), trains in seconds, and sets the bar every fancier model must beat. Deep learning on 50k tabular rows adds opacity without payoff; clustering doesn't predict the label.
scenarios.hint: What does marketing need besides a prediction?

scenarios.title: Math Without Tears
scenarios.situation: You want to learn ML but the math is intimidating — matrices and probability from years ago. You learn best by doing, not by reading proofs.
scenarios.prompt: How do you build the math you actually need?
evidence: the gap
Rusty on linear algebra and probability; strong on spreadsheets and business logic.
the style
Learns by building — proofs put you to sleep.
choices: Learn just-in-time through geometric intuition plus code: vectors as arrows, dot products as similarity, gradient descent as 'walk downhill' — proofs later, if ever.
Complete a full proof-based linear algebra course before touching ML.
Memorize the formulas without implementing them.
Skip the math entirely — the libraries handle everything.
scenarios.why: You need working intuition, not theorems: enough linear algebra to read shapes and similarity, enough probability to reason about uncertainty, enough calculus to picture gradient descent. Code-grounded intuition ('plot it, perturb it, watch it') sticks for builders; proofs-first filters out exactly the practitioners ML needs.
scenarios.hint: Do you need to prove the theorem, or use it correctly?

scenarios.title: The Unreproducible Notebook
scenarios.situation: A colleague's notebook scores 0.91 for them but 0.84 when you re-run it. During exploration they ran cells out of order, and no random seeds are set anywhere.
scenarios.prompt: What is the root cause, and the fix?
evidence: the habit
Cells executed out of order during exploration — hidden state everywhere.
the seeds
None set — train_test_split and model init vary run to run.
choices: Restart the kernel and Run All to surface order-dependence; then fix cell order, set random seeds, and refactor stable logic into a script.
Accept 0.84 as the true score and move on.
Average the two runs and report 0.875.
Reinstall the libraries — the environment must differ.
scenarios.why: Out-of-order execution leaves hidden state: variables from a deleted experiment still in memory, making the 0.91 irreproducible. 'Restart and Run All' is the reproducibility test every notebook must pass. Seeds remove the remaining randomness, and scripts remove the temptation to run cells out of order.
scenarios.hint: Would a completely fresh kernel reproduce the 0.91?

scenarios.title: 200 Features, 300 Rows
scenarios.situation: A colleague trained gradient boosting with 200 features on 300 rows, no validation set, and proudly reports 0.99 training accuracy. They want to ship it.
scenarios.prompt: What is your advice?
evidence: the setup
200 features, 300 rows — more dimensions than samples.
the evidence
0.99 on training data; no held-out validation at all.
choices: It's almost surely overfit: add a validation split, cut features aggressively, or switch to a simpler regularized model.
Add more features to capture the signal the model is clearly finding.
Tune hyperparameters harder on the training set to push past 0.99.
Ship it — 0.99 is 0.99.
scenarios.why: With more features than rows, any flexible model can memorize the training set — 0.99 measures memorization, not learning. Training accuracy without validation is not evidence of anything. The fixes all reduce capacity or measure honestly: fewer features, regularization, cross-validation, and a simpler model class.
scenarios.hint: What would the score be on data the model has never seen?

scenarios.title: The Loop That Ate the Afternoon
scenarios.situation: Your churn feature script uses df.iterrows() to compute a per-customer recency feature across 2.4M rows. It has been running for three hours and your laptop fan sounds like a jet. A senior ML engineer glances at it and says 'vectorize it.' You have 30 minutes before the pipeline review.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right fix, and why does it work?
choices: Replace the row-wise loop with a vectorized pandas/numpy operation (e.g., groupby transform or arithmetic on whole columns) — the work moves into compiled C code instead of the Python interpreter
Buy a bigger machine and let the loop finish — hardware solves slow code
Sample the data down to 10% so the loop finishes fast — fewer rows, same features
Rewrite the loop in pure Python with a for loop over df.itertuples() — itertuples is faster than iterrows and the logic stays identical
scenarios.why: iterrows() pays Python-interpreter overhead per row; vectorized ops push the loop into compiled C, typically 50-100x faster. itertuples() only trims overhead, it does not remove it. Sampling changes the features (and the model), and bigger hardware just makes slow code expensive.
scenarios.hint: Where does the per-row cost actually live — in your logic, or in the interpreter running it?
evidence: Rewrote an iterrows loop as a vectorized op with a measured speedup

scenarios.title: Same Code, Different Score
scenarios.situation: You demo your first gradient-boosting model: AUC 0.81. Your mentor re-runs the exact notebook and gets 0.77. You re-run it yourself and get 0.83. Nothing in the code changed between runs. The stakeholder meeting is tomorrow and you cannot explain the number.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely cause, and what is the durable fix?
choices: Floating-point nondeterminism across CPUs — pin the exact CPU model for all runs
Unseeded randomness: train_test_split, the model, and any shuffling each draw fresh random numbers per run — set random_state everywhere, pin library versions, and log the seed with the run
The data file is being modified by another process between runs — lock the file
Jupyter caches stale cell outputs — restart the kernel and rerun once
scenarios.why: Unseeded RNGs in the split, the estimator, and resampling make every run a different experiment; 0.77–0.83 swings are expected noise, not a bug. Seeding everything plus pinned versions makes the run reproducible. CPU float differences are real but tiny compared to RNG draws; file locking and kernel restarts miss the actual mechanism.
scenarios.hint: What in the code draws random numbers without being told which ones?
evidence: Made an ML notebook fully reproducible with seeds and a locked environment

scenarios.title: The Warning You Ignored
scenarios.situation: Your feature script does: filtered = df[df['active']]; filtered['recency'] = ... . pandas prints SettingWithCopyWarning. You ignore it — 'just a warning.' Later, the recency feature is missing for 30% of customers in the training matrix, silently, and the model trains on the corrupted frame.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct response to this warning?
choices: Suppress it with pd.options.mode.chained_assignment = None — warnings are noise

Treat it as the bug it is: chained assignment (df[mask]['col'] = x) may write to a temporary COPY, silently dropping your assignment — fix with explicit .loc (df.loc[mask, 'col'] = x) or an explicit .copy(); in ML pipelines, 'sometimes works' assignment is a data-corruption vector, never suppress it
Restart the kernel — warnings are often stale
Use .apply instead — apply doesn't warn
scenarios.why: SettingWithCopyWarning signals ambiguous write semantics: pandas can't guarantee whether you're modifying the original or a copy, so the assignment SOMETIMES silently fails — the worst kind of bug (nondeterministic data corruption). .loc makes the target explicit; .copy() makes the object explicit. Suppressing it converts a caught bug into an uncaught one.
scenarios.hint: When pandas says 'a value is trying to be set on a copy,' what happens to your feature values?
evidence: Eliminated SettingWithCopyWarning with explicit .loc indexing

domains.name: Systems Anatomy: Seeing Systems as Living Flows
domains.description: Learn to see Data Analyst To Ml as living systems — not static diagrams, but moving sequences where every part connects. Master systems thinking for exams and interviews.

scenarios.title: The Analyst to ML Path Mystery
scenarios.situation: Users report that Analyst to ML Path is not working correctly. The obvious checks pass — the components are online, basic connectivity works. You need to think in systems, not symptoms.
scenarios.prompt: Using the systems anatomy method (whole → cut open → step through → pull apart), how would you systematically trace a failure in Analyst to ML Path?
choices: Walk the full journey: start from the trigger, verify each handoff in sequence, check dependencies at every step, and isolate where the flow breaks — then examine that specific layer
Restart all components — Analyst to ML Path issues are always fixed by restarting
Check the most common cause from memory and apply that fix immediately
Escalate to senior support — Analyst to ML Path is too complex to troubleshoot systematically
scenarios.why: The correct answer is A. Systems thinking means tracing the living flow: (1) Whole: what is Analyst to ML Path supposed to do end-to-end? (2) Cut open: what are the layers/stages? (3) Step through: verify each handoff — where does the expected output diverge from actual? (4) Pull apart: isolate the broken layer and examine it in detail. This method works for any Analyst to ML Path failure in Data Analyst To Ml.
scenarios.hint: Don't jump to the fix. First map the journey, then find where it breaks.
objectives: Apply systems anatomy to Analyst to ML Path
evidence: System Status
All Analyst to ML Path components report 'online'. Basic health checks pass.
User Report
Functionality is broken despite green status indicators. The failure is in the flow, not the components.

scenarios.title: Where Does Validation Live?
scenarios.situation: You are tracing a training-loop diagram: data loader → forward pass → loss → backward pass → optimizer step, repeating per batch. Your teammate added early stopping 'to prevent overfitting,' but validation loss is checked inside the batch loop, right after every optimizer step, and training halts the moment it ticks upward once.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this training-loop anatomy?
choices: Early stopping should watch training loss instead — it is smoother and cheaper to compute
Nothing — checking validation after every step is the most rigorous possible early stopping

Validation belongs at epoch boundaries on a held-out set, with patience over several epochs: per-batch checks react to noise, and a single upward tick is not a trend — this stops training almost immediately on noise
Validation should happen before the forward pass so the model sees it during training
scenarios.why: Batch-level validation loss is dominated by sampling noise; stopping on one uptick aborts training prematurely. The correct anatomy: train on batches, evaluate on the full validation set at epoch end, and stop only after N epochs (patience) without improvement, restoring the best checkpoint. Watching training loss defeats the purpose — training loss always goes down.
scenarios.hint: Is one batch's validation loss a signal or noise? What would patience change?
objectives: Trace the training loop's validation stage
Apply early stopping with patience correctly
evidence: Diagrammed a training loop and placed validation + early stopping at the right stage

scenarios.title: The Skew Enters Here
scenarios.situation: Your model's offline AUC is 0.86 but production is 0.71. The feature pipeline has two paths: a nightly batch job (Python/pandas) that builds training features, and a real-time service (Java) that computes the same features at request time. The model, the data source, and the feature definitions document are identical on both sides.
scenarios.prompt: Where does training-serving skew enter this anatomy, and what is the fix?
choices: Production traffic is just harder — accept the 0.15 gap as normal
The feature definitions document is out of date — rewrite the docs
The model file is corrupted in production — re-export and redeploy it

The two implementations of the 'same' features diverge: pandas and Java handle nulls, rounding, timezones, or edge cases differently, so the model sees different inputs live than it trained on — unify on one shared transformation (shared code, feature store, or single-language pipeline)
scenarios.why: Training-serving skew almost always lives in duplicated transformation logic: two codebases implementing 'the same' feature will disagree on nulls, rounding, and edge cases. The model then scores inputs drawn from a different distribution than training. Docs do not fix code divergence; the fix is a single source of truth for transformations.
scenarios.hint: Same definition, two languages, two codebases — what could possibly differ?
objectives: Locate training-serving skew in a feature pipeline
evidence: Audited a dual-path feature pipeline and named the skew entry point

scenarios.title: Chasing p99
scenarios.situation: Your real-time fraud model must score in under 100ms at p99. The serving path is: API gateway → feature service (3 downstream lookups) → model inference → rules post-processing → response. Profiling shows: lookups 62ms, inference 8ms, post-processing 11ms, gateway overhead 6ms. Leadership wants a faster GPU model to fix latency.
scenarios.prompt: What should you actually optimize?
choices: The feature lookups: at 62ms they dominate the budget, and a faster model cannot fix them — cache hot features, parallelize the lookups, or precompute; the model is only 8ms of an 87ms path
The API gateway — 6ms of pure overhead is unacceptable
Post-processing rules — rewrite them in a faster language
The model — GPU inference will cut the 8ms substantially
scenarios.why: Latency anatomy says optimize the dominant stage: 62ms of lookups vs 8ms of inference. Even free inference saves only 8ms. Caching, parallel fan-out, or precomputed features attack the real bottleneck. A GPU upgrade is the classic misdiagnosis — optimizing the stage that is already fast.
scenarios.hint: Add up the stages. Which one owns the budget?
objectives: Decompose a serving path by latency stage
Target optimization at the dominant stage
evidence: Profiled a serving path and identified the true latency bottleneck

scenarios.title: The Run You Cannot Reproduce
scenarios.situation: Six weeks ago a contractor trained the churn model now in production. The notebook exists. The AUC was 0.84. You need to retrain with fresh data, but your retrain scores 0.79 and nobody can explain the gap. The notebook has no logged dataset version, no code commit reference, no hyperparameters recorded, and no random seed.
scenarios.prompt: What is the minimum experiment-tracking anatomy that would have prevented this?
choices: A longer notebook with more markdown explaining each cell

Every run logs: dataset version (or hash), code commit, hyperparameters, random seed, environment versions, and resulting metrics — the full lineage needed to replay the run; without it, 'retrain' is a guess, not a reproduction
A shared drive folder where everyone saves their final model.pkl
Weekly team demos so knowledge is shared verbally
scenarios.why: Reproducibility requires the complete run lineage: data version, code version, hyperparameters, seed, environment. The notebook alone captures none of the five reliably. Markdown and demos document intent, not state; a model.pkl without lineage cannot be regenerated or audited. Experiment tracking exists precisely so a retrain is a replay, not archaeology.
scenarios.hint: To replay a run you need every input that could change the output. List them.
objectives: Enumerate the artifacts of a reproducible run
evidence: Listed the full lineage needed to reproduce a training run

scenarios.title: Three Doors for Leakage
scenarios.situation: Your pipeline: (1) ingest 2 years of orders, (2) compute customer aggregates (avg order value, total spend), (3) split into train/test by customer, (4) scale features with StandardScaler, (5) train. A reviewer flags three suspects: A — aggregates computed before the split; B — scaler fit on train only; C — split by customer instead of by time.
scenarios.prompt: Which is the real leakage path, and why?
choices: A is fine and C is fine; the pipeline is clean
B — the scaler must be fit on the full dataset for stability

A — aggregates computed before the split let each customer's statistics leak across the train/test boundary is not the issue; the real problem is subtler: aggregates are fine pre-split IF the split is by customer and aggregates use only that customer's own history. The actual leak: none of A/B/C as described — but wait, recheck A: aggregates include each customer's full 2-year history, and the prediction is 'will churn next quarter' — aggregates built from the whole window include post-prediction-period behavior
C — splitting by customer is always leakage; only time splits are valid
scenarios.why: The leak is temporal, not split-mechanical: aggregates computed over the full 2-year window include behavior from AFTER the prediction moment (e.g., 'total spend' includes orders placed after the churn-prediction date). The model learns from the future. Split-by-customer is legitimate when the task is 'new customers'; scaler-fit-on-train-only is correct practice. Point-in-time correctness — 'was this knowable at prediction time?' — is the audit that catches it.
scenarios.hint: Forget the split mechanics for a second — ask what time period each aggregate covers versus when the prediction is made.
evidence: Audited a pipeline and separated real leakage from false alarms

scenarios.title: The Silent Gradients
scenarios.situation: You built a 12-layer feedforward network for tabular data (an experiment, against advice). Training loss barely moves after epoch 2. You log gradient norms per layer: layer 12 (output side) shows healthy norms around 1e-2; layer 1 (input side) shows 1e-9. Activations are sigmoids throughout.
scenarios.prompt: What does the gradient-flow anatomy tell you, and what is the fix?
choices: The optimizer is stuck in a local minimum — switch to a different optimizer
The data needs more feature engineering — gradients are fine, features are weak
The learning rate is too high — gradients are exploding; reduce it 10x

Vanishing gradients: repeated multiplication through saturating sigmoid derivatives shrinks the signal to ~0 by the input layers, so early layers never learn — switch to ReLU activations (and consider batch norm / residual connections / a shallower net)
scenarios.why: Gradient norms decaying 1e-2 → 1e-9 across layers is the textbook vanishing-gradient signature: each sigmoid layer multiplies by a derivative ≤ 0.25, so the signal dies before reaching early layers. ReLU's derivative (0 or 1) preserves magnitude. Learning-rate and optimizer changes cannot fix a signal that never arrives; the architecture/activation is the anatomy at fault.
scenarios.hint: Follow the gradient backward layer by layer — what multiplies it at each sigmoid?
objectives: Read per-layer gradient norms as a diagnostic
evidence: Diagnosed vanishing gradients from layer-wise norm logs

scenarios.title: The Model That Eats Its Own Tail
scenarios.situation: Your fraud model works well: it blocks suspicious transactions in real time. Six months later, retraining on recent data, performance drops. You realize: blocked fraud never completes, so recent training data contains almost no confirmed fraud examples — the model's own actions erased the signal it learns from. Meanwhile the fraudsters adapted to the blocks.
scenarios.prompt: What is this systems failure, and how do you break the loop?
choices: A feedback loop (performative prediction): the model's decisions shape its future training data, censoring the positive class and hiding adversary adaptation — break it with exploration (allow a scored sample through for labeling), human-reviewed holdout labels, and monitoring the blocked population separately
Concept drift — just retrain more frequently on the recent data
Underfitting — use a larger model that can learn from less fraud signal
Label noise — pay analysts to relabel the recent data more carefully
scenarios.why: This is a feedback loop, not drift or noise: the deployment's actions censor the training signal (blocked fraud never becomes a labeled example), and retraining on censored data bakes in the blindness. More frequent retraining on the same censored data makes it worse. The fix restores ground truth outside the loop: exploration traffic, independent labeling, and separate monitoring of the intervened population.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the labels when the model's predictions change reality?
evidence: Diagrammed a feedback loop between model actions and training data
