scenarios.title: Trees First, Deep Later
scenarios.situation: You have 40,000 rows of tabular customer data (tenure, spend, plan type, support contacts) and a churn label. Your stakeholder read that neural networks are 'state of the art' and wants one. You have two weeks and a laptop.
scenarios.prompt: Which algorithm family should you start with, and why?
choices: A deep neural network — it is state of the art, so it will beat anything else on any data
Gradient-boosted trees (or random forest): they dominate tabular data at this scale, train fast on CPU, need little tuning, and give feature importances you can explain to stakeholders
k-means clustering — unsupervised first, labels later
Linear regression — simplest possible, always the right start
scenarios.why: On medium-size tabular data, gradient boosting routinely matches or beats neural nets with a fraction of the effort and compute — and it trains on a laptop in minutes. Neural nets earn their keep on images, text, and massive datasets, not 40k-row tables. Start where the expected value is highest; escalate only if trees plateau.
scenarios.hint: What data shape made neural nets famous — and is that your data shape?
objectives: Match algorithm family to data type and scale
evidence: Justified a starting algorithm from data characteristics, not trends

scenarios.title: The Shuffled Timeline
scenarios.situation: You split two years of subscription data randomly into train/test and get AUC 0.90. Your mentor asks one question: 'What date does your test set cover?' You check — test rows are interleaved across the full two years, including months before most training rows.
scenarios.prompt: What is wrong with this split, and what should replace it?
choices: You need stratification, not a time split — the class balance drifted
Nothing — random splits are the gold standard; interleaving is fine

Random splitting leaks the future: the model trains on later behavior to predict earlier behavior, which never happens in production — use a time-based split (train on the past, test on the most recent period)
The split ratio is wrong — use 50/50 instead of 80/20
scenarios.why: In production the model always predicts the future from the past; a random split lets it 'learn' from future rows, inflating the score. A time-based split reproduces the real deployment condition — train on months 1–18, test on 19–24. Stratification fixes class balance, not temporal leakage.
scenarios.hint: In production, which direction does time flow relative to the prediction?
objectives: Detect temporal leakage in random splits
evidence: Replaced a random split with a time-based split and explained the score change

scenarios.title: The 99/72 Split
scenarios.situation: Your random forest scores 99% accuracy on training data and 72% on validation. Your first instinct is to add more features and tune hyperparameters for a week. Your mentor suggests you look at the learning curves first: training error near zero, validation error high and flat as data grows.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnosis, and what is the highest-leverage fix?
choices: Bad luck — reshuffle the split and the gap will close
The validation set is too small — the 72% is just noise
Underfitting — the model is too simple; add depth and features
Overfitting (high variance): the model memorized training noise — constrain it (limit depth, add regularization, or get more training data) rather than adding complexity
scenarios.why: A large train/validation gap with near-zero training error is the classic overfitting signature: the model has capacity to memorize. Adding features or depth feeds the problem. The learning curve (validation error flat as data grows) says more data would help, but the immediate lever is reducing capacity — shallower trees, min-samples constraints, or regularization.
scenarios.hint: Training error near zero + big gap = the model learned what, exactly?
evidence: Read a learning curve and prescribed the correct bias/variance fix

scenarios.title: Beating Nothing
scenarios.situation: Your churn model hits 88% accuracy and the team celebrates. Then someone checks the base rate: 12% of customers churn, so predicting 'nobody churns' scores 88% without any model at all. Your model is exactly as useful as doing nothing.
scenarios.prompt: What baseline discipline should have caught this on day one?
choices: Always build the dumb baseline first (majority class, mean prediction, simple heuristic) and require every model to beat it by a meaningful margin — a model that ties 'predict nothing' has learned nothing
Compare only against other ML models — baselines are not real models
Use a harder metric instead of a baseline — metrics replace baselines
Skip baselines — they waste time that could go to tuning
scenarios.why: The baseline is the honesty anchor: majority-class here scores 88% for free, so the model's 88% is zero value-add. Every project should start with the dumbest reasonable predictor and demand the real model clear it by a margin that justifies its complexity. A better metric alone would not have revealed that the model adds nothing over doing nothing.
scenarios.hint: What is the cheapest possible predictor — and what does it score?
objectives: Judge models against value-add, not raw scores
evidence: Built a baseline first and measured the model's marginal gain over it

scenarios.title: The Cost of Being Wrong
scenarios.situation: Your transaction-risk model flags suspicious payments. A missed fraud costs the company $500 on average; a false alarm costs an analyst 2 minutes (about $1.50) to review. The model at the default 0.5 threshold catches 60% of fraud with 5% false alarms. Finance asks: 'Is this the right operating point?'
scenarios.prompt: How should you set the threshold?
choices: Keep 0.5 — it is the default for a reason and changing it looks arbitrary

Lower the threshold to catch more fraud: at $500 per miss vs $1.50 per false alarm, misses are ~300x costlier, so favor recall heavily — pick the threshold that minimizes expected business cost, not the default
Raise the threshold to 0.9 — fewer false alarms means happier analysts
Optimize for accuracy — the threshold that maximizes accuracy is definitionally best
scenarios.why: The threshold is a business decision, not a statistical default: expected cost = P(miss)×$500 + P(false alarm)×$1.50. With misses 300x costlier, the optimal threshold sits far below 0.5, trading cheap reviews for expensive catches. Accuracy-maximization ignores the asymmetric costs entirely.
scenarios.hint: Multiply each error type by its price tag. Which error can you afford more of?
objectives: Convert error costs into threshold decisions
evidence: Set a classification threshold from explicit business costs

scenarios.title: What Are We Predicting, Exactly?
scenarios.situation: The brief says 'predict churn.' You could frame it as classification ('will churn in the next 30 days: yes/no') or regression ('days until cancellation'). The retention team runs monthly campaigns and wants a ranked call list; finance wants expected revenue loss per customer.
scenarios.prompt: How do you choose the problem framing?
choices: Let the algorithm decide — framing does not matter much
Regression — predicting exact days is strictly more informative than yes/no

Classification on a fixed horizon ('churn in next 30 days'): it matches the campaign cadence, gives a clean ranked list with calibrated probabilities, and avoids the censoring headaches of time-to-event regression on customers who never churn
Predict both and average them — more models is more robust
scenarios.why: Framing follows the decision it serves: the retention team acts monthly on a ranked list, which fixed-horizon classification delivers directly with interpretable probabilities. Time-to-event regression sounds richer but most customers never churn (censored targets), adding modeling complexity for a decision nobody asked for. Match the target to the action.
scenarios.hint: What decision will consume the prediction — and what shape does that decision need?
objectives: Frame ML problems from the downstream decision
evidence: Reframed a vague 'predict X' brief into a decision-shaped target

scenarios.title: More Data or Better Model?
scenarios.situation: You have 5,000 labeled support tickets and a classifier plateaued at 0.78 F1 after tuning. Labeling 5,000 more costs $4,000 and two weeks. A teammate wants to spend the two weeks on architecture experiments instead. The learning curve shows validation error still dropping as training size grows.
scenarios.prompt: Where should the two weeks go?
choices: Neither — 0.78 is fine; ship it
Collect more UNLABELED data — volume alone helps supervised models
Architecture experiments — tuning is free and data is expensive
More labeled data: the still-falling learning curve says the model is data-starved (high variance), so additional labels buy more than another tuning round — spend the $4k where the curve points
scenarios.why: The learning curve is the decision instrument: validation error still falling with more data means variance dominates, and the highest-ROI move is more labels. Architecture search helps when the curve has flattened (bias problem). Unlabeled data does not move a supervised curve. Read the curve, then spend.
scenarios.hint: What does a still-falling validation curve tell you about the bottleneck?
objectives: Use learning curves to allocate effort
Weigh data labeling vs model tuning ROI
evidence: Used a learning curve to justify a data-vs-tuning decision

scenarios.title: The Interpretable Baseline
scenarios.situation: Compliance needs to approve your credit-risk model, and the first question will be: 'Why did it decline THIS applicant?' Your random forest gives great AUC but its 'explanation' is 500 trees voting. The deadline is in two weeks.
scenarios.prompt: Which modeling choice serves both accuracy and auditability?
choices: Ship the forest — accuracy beats explainability, compliance will adapt

Start with logistic regression (or a shallow decision tree): coefficients ARE the explanation ('income below X and delinquencies above Y drove the decision'), it is a strong baseline on tabular data, and you can quantify exactly what the forest buys over it — if the gap is small, ship the interpretable one
Build a neural network with an attention layer — attention is explanation
Average all three — ensembles are always safer
scenarios.why: Regulated decisions need reason-giving, not just accuracy: logistic coefficients map directly to 'why this applicant,' which is what the audit asks. The baseline also prices the complexity — if the forest only buys +0.01 AUC, the interpretable model wins on total value. 'Attention as explanation' does not survive a compliance review.
scenarios.hint: What question will the auditor ask — and which model can answer it in one sentence?
objectives: Choose interpretable models for regulated decisions
evidence: Selected a model family to satisfy an auditability requirement

scenarios.title: The Tabular Default
scenarios.situation: New project: 300,000 rows, 60 mixed-type tabular features, binary label. The team debates for a week: random forest vs gradient boosting vs 'a small neural net, because deep learning.' Nobody has run a single experiment.
scenarios.prompt: How do you settle the algorithm debate?
choices: Pick random forest — it is the safest default, no experiment needed
Debate until consensus — the choice matters too much to rush

Run the cheap experiment: logistic regression baseline, random forest, and gradient boosting (histogram-based, e.g., LightGBM/XGBoost) with default-ish params on a time-boxed afternoon — on tabular data at this scale, boosting usually wins; let 4 hours of evidence end the week of debate
Go straight to the neural net — settle it by ambition
scenarios.why: Algorithm debates are cheap to resolve empirically: a time-boxed bake-off on the actual data beats a week of opinions. The expected outcome (boosting ≥ forest > linear on tabular) is well-established, but the experiment also surfaces data-specific surprises (leakage, metric quirks) that debate never finds. Evidence ends arguments; defaults without evidence are just opinions with seniority.
scenarios.hint: What costs more — an afternoon of experiments, or another week of meetings?
objectives: Default to boosting for tabular data
evidence: Ran a 3-model bake-off and chose from evidence, not debate

scenarios.title: Knobs That Matter
scenarios.situation: Your gradient-boosting model has 15 hyperparameters. A teammate launches a 3-day grid search over all of them. You have a hunch most knobs barely matter — but 'hunch' is not an argument.
scenarios.prompt: How should hyperparameter effort be allocated?
choices: Tune one parameter at a time exhaustively — coordinate descent is principled
Skip tuning — defaults are fine for every problem
Grid-search everything — thoroughness is rigor

Prioritize the high-leverage knobs: learning rate + number of trees (the core bias/variance trade), tree depth / min-child-weight (capacity), and subsample rates — tune those with randomized search (broader coverage per run than grid), and leave the rest at sane defaults; most gains come from 3–4 parameters
scenarios.why: Hyperparameter importance is heavily skewed: learning rate, tree count, and depth drive most of the variance in outcomes; the rest are fine-tuning. Randomized search beats grid because it explores more distinct values of the important knobs per run. Three days of full-grid is mostly compute spent learning that 11 knobs don't matter — on this dataset, at this time.
scenarios.hint: If you could only tune THREE knobs, which three move the needle?
evidence: Tuned the top-4 knobs with randomized search and justified the rest as defaults

scenarios.title: Bagging vs Boosting
scenarios.situation: Two ensemble proposals for a noisy sensor-failure dataset: (A) random forest (bagging: many deep trees on bootstrap samples, averaged), (B) gradient boosting (sequential shallow trees correcting errors). The data is noisy — labels are unreliable ~10% of the time.
scenarios.prompt: Which ensemble fits noisy labels, and why?
choices: Bagging (random forest): it reduces VARIANCE by averaging independent trees, which tames noise; boosting reduces BIAS by chasing errors sequentially — and with 10% label noise, boosting will chase mislabeled points as if they were signal, overfitting the noise
Whichever trains faster — speed is the tiebreaker
Neither — ensembles can't handle label noise
Boosting — it is strictly stronger than bagging on every dataset
scenarios.why: The bias/variance framing picks the tool: bagging averages away variance (noise), boosting attacks bias (underfitting) by fixating on mistakes. Noisy labels turn boosting's strength into a weakness — it diligently learns the mislabeled points. Match the ensemble to the error type: noisy → bagging; underfit → boosting.
scenarios.hint: What does each ensemble do with a point the model gets 'wrong' — and what if the point's label is the thing that's wrong?
objectives: Reason about label noise in boosting
evidence: Chose bagging vs boosting from a noise analysis

scenarios.title: When Deep Earns Its Keep
scenarios.situation: Two new projects land: (P1) 2M product images to classify into 500 categories; (P2) 80,000 rows of tabular loan data. One engineer says 'deep learning for both — it's the modern approach.' You have limited GPU budget.
scenarios.prompt: Where does deep learning earn the GPU budget?
choices: Both — modern problems deserve modern methods

P1 (images): deep learning's advantage is representation learning on raw perceptual data — CNNs/ViTs discover features (edges → textures → objects) that hand-engineering cannot match at 2M images / 500 classes; P2 (tabular) stays with gradient boosting, which wins or ties at far lower cost
P2 — tabular data is simpler so deep learning will crush it
Neither — deep learning is overhyped everywhere
scenarios.why: Deep learning's edge is specific: learning representations from raw, high-dimensional perceptual data (images, audio, text) where manual features fail. On tabular data, the features are already meaningful columns and boosting dominates — a neural net just burns GPU to rediscover what the columns already say. Spend the GPU where representation learning is the bottleneck.
scenarios.hint: In which project are the 'features' raw pixels vs already-meaningful columns?
objectives: Allocate deep learning to representation-learning problems
evidence: Justified a deep-vs-shallow choice from data modality

scenarios.title: The Distance Trap
scenarios.situation: Your kNN prototype on customer data (features: annual revenue in dollars, tenure in years, login count) performs terribly. Switching to a random forest 'fixes' it. A teammate concludes 'kNN is just bad.' You suspect the algorithm was never given a fair fight.
scenarios.prompt: What was kNN's actual problem?
choices: The data needs more rows — kNN is data-hungry
kNN is obsolete — the teammate is right

Unscaled features: revenue (millions) dominates the distance computation, making tenure and logins invisible — kNN/SVM measure Euclidean distance, so features must be on comparable scales; the forest 'fixed' it only because trees are scale-invariant, masking the preprocessing bug
k is too small — always use k=100
scenarios.why: Distance-based methods inherit the units: a $1M revenue difference swamps a 3-year tenure difference in Euclidean space, so 'nearest' means 'nearest in revenue.' Scaling (standardization) puts features on comparable footing — the actual fix. The forest masked the bug via scale-invariance, which is why 'algorithm B beats algorithm A' sometimes means 'pipeline suited B better.'
scenarios.hint: What does 'nearest' mean when one feature ranges over millions and another over single digits?
objectives: Diagnose scaling failures in distance methods
Separate algorithm weakness from pipeline mismatch
evidence: Fixed a kNN model by diagnosing the scaling problem

scenarios.title: The Humble Baseline Wins
scenarios.situation: Ticket-routing text classification, 12,000 labeled tickets, 8 categories. The team wants to fine-tune a transformer (2 weeks). You quietly try Multinomial Naive Bayes on TF-IDF in 20 minutes: 0.81 F1. The transformer advocate says 'Naive Bayes is a toy.'
scenarios.prompt: What is Naive Bayes' proper role here?
choices: Use it as the production model permanently — simple always wins
Only use it for binary problems — it can't do 8 categories
None — it is a toy; go straight to transformers

The honest baseline that prices the transformer: 0.81 in 20 minutes sets the bar — if 2 weeks of fine-tuning buys +0.02, the business case fails; Naive Bayes' independence assumption is 'naive' but its word-count likelihoods are a strong, fast signal for text, and it trains before the GPU instance even boots
scenarios.why: Naive Bayes on TF-IDF is the classic text baseline: embarrassingly fast, surprisingly strong, and it quantifies exactly what sophistication must beat. The 'toy' dismissal skips the ROI question — the 2-week investment needs a measured prize, and 0.81-in-20-minutes is the measuring stick. Baselines don't have to win; they have to price the win.
scenarios.hint: What does the transformer need to beat — and by how much to justify 2 weeks?
objectives: Use Naive Bayes as a text baseline
evidence: Built a Naive Bayes text baseline and used it to scope further work

scenarios.title: How Many Segments?
scenarios.situation: Marketing wants customer segments from behavioral data. You run k-means with k=5 because '5 feels right.' The clusters: one giant blob (70% of customers), three slivers, and one cluster with 12 customers. Marketing can't use them — the segments don't correspond to anything actionable.
scenarios.prompt: What is the rigorous approach to k-means segmentation?
choices: Combine quantitative and qualitative validation: elbow/silhouette scores across k to find structure, stability checks across seeds, AND the business test — can marketing name each segment and act differently on it? A statistically 'optimal' k that produces unusable segments fails the actual job; iterate k with the stakeholder in the loop
k=5 is industry standard — the problem is the data, not k
Switch to hierarchical clustering — it chooses k automatically
Try k=3, 4, 6, 7... until one 'looks right' — visual inspection is standard
scenarios.why: k-means will always return k clusters, meaningful or not — the algorithm cannot tell you k. Elbow/silhouette detect geometric structure, but segmentation's customer is a human team: segments must be describable and actionable. The giant-blob result also hints at scaling or outlier issues to fix first. Validate with both statistics and the stakeholder's ability to USE the answer.
scenarios.hint: Who consumes the segments — and what makes a segment usable to them?
objectives: Validate k-means with metrics + business usability
evidence: Chose k with elbow/silhouette plus stakeholder usability review

domains.name: Feature Engineering
domains.description: The highest-leverage ML skill: turning raw columns into signals models can actually learn from.

scenarios.title: The Model That Was Too Good
scenarios.situation: Your churn model hits 0.97 AUC in validation. In the first production month, it performs barely above random. The features include 'days_since_last_login', 'support_tickets_30d', and 'cancellation_page_visits'.
scenarios.prompt: What is the most likely failure?
choices: The model overfit — add regularization and retrain

Target leakage: 'cancellation_page_visits' (and possibly ticket text) contains information only knowable AFTER the churn decision started — the model learned the future. Audit every feature for point-in-time validity; drop or lag the leakers
Concept drift — the customer base changed in a month
The validation split was too small
scenarios.why: 0.97 offline → random online is the leakage signature, not overfitting (overfit degrades modestly, not catastrophically). Cancellation-page visits happen DURING churn — at prediction time (say, 30 days before), that signal does not exist yet. The model learned 'people who visit the cancel page churn' — true and useless. Every temporal feature needs the audit question: 'was this knowable at prediction time?'
scenarios.hint: Which feature could only exist after the outcome began? What does 0.97→random tell you?
evidence: Validation
AUC 0.97, precision/recall excellent.
Production m1
AUC 0.54. Feature audit: cancellation_page_visits populated 0-3 days before churn label date.

scenarios.title: The Column From the Future
scenarios.situation: Your subscription-churn model features include 'refund_amount' — the refund issued when a customer cancels. Validation AUC is 0.94. In the feature audit you notice refunds are timestamped 0–2 days AFTER the cancellation event, while predictions are supposed to run 30 days BEFORE cancellation.
scenarios.prompt: What is the verdict on this feature?
choices: Drop it (or lag it): the refund is only knowable after the outcome — it is target leakage, and the 0.94 is the model 'predicting' the past, which will collapse in production
Keep it but reduce its weight with regularization
Replace it with the refund reason code — same signal, less leakage
Keep it — 0.94 AUC proves it is the best feature
scenarios.why: A feature timestamped after the prediction moment is definitionally leakage: at scoring time (30 days pre-churn) the refund does not exist yet. The 0.94 measures hindsight, not foresight. Regularization cannot fix a feature that will be null in production; the reason code has the same timing problem. The audit question — 'was this knowable at prediction time?' — is the whole verdict.
scenarios.hint: At the moment the model scores a customer, does this column have a value yet?
evidence: Flagged a leaking feature by comparing feature and prediction timestamps

scenarios.title: 47,000 ZIP Codes
scenarios.situation: You want to use customer ZIP code (47,000 distinct values) in a churn model with 60,000 rows. One-hot encoding would add 47,000 sparse columns. Your first attempt melts the laptop. A teammate suggests 'just label-encode it as integers 1–47000.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the right encoding strategy?
choices: One-hot encode anyway — sparsity is fine, get more RAM

Target encoding with cross-validation (or smoothing): replace each ZIP with its historical churn rate, computed inside CV folds so the target does not leak — it compresses 47k categories into one informative numeric column
Drop ZIP entirely — high-cardinality features are never worth it
Label-encode as integers — one column, problem solved
scenarios.why: Label-encoding invents a false ordinal (ZIP 90210 is not 'greater than' 10001), which tree splits and linear models will misread. One-hot on 47k values explodes dimensionality on 60k rows. Target encoding captures the actual signal (churn rate by area) in one column — but it must be computed within cross-validation folds, or the target leaks into the feature.
scenarios.hint: What does the integer 90210 mean to a model — and is that meaning true?
objectives: Prevent target leakage in target encoding
evidence: Encoded a high-cardinality feature without leakage or dimension explosion

scenarios.title: To Scale or Not to Scale
scenarios.situation: Your pipeline StandardScales every numeric feature before a random forest. A colleague's kNN prototype on the same data performs terribly until scaled, then beats the forest. You are now choosing the preprocessing for the production pipeline, which may serve either model.
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct scaling decision?
choices: Scale only the features with large values, like revenue
Scale everything always — scaling never hurts

Trees are scale-invariant (splits only care about order), so scaling is wasted work for the forest; distance-based models (kNN, SVM, regularized linear models, neural nets) REQUIRE scaling — make scaling part of the model-specific pipeline (e.g., ColumnTransformer), not a global preprocessing step
Never scale — raw units are more interpretable
scenarios.why: Scaling is model-dependent, not data-dependent: tree splits compare values within one feature, so monotonic rescaling changes nothing; kNN distances are dominated by large-magnitude features without it. A global 'scale everything' step is harmless for trees but hides the real requirement — and if the scaler is fit outside the model pipeline it becomes a serving-skew risk. Tie preprocessing to the estimator.
scenarios.hint: What does each algorithm actually DO with the numbers — compare, or measure distance?
objectives: Match scaling decisions to algorithm mechanics
evidence: Justified a scaling choice from the algorithm's math, not habit

scenarios.title: 400 Features, 2,000 Rows
scenarios.situation: An upstream team hands you a dataset with 400 engineered features and 2,000 labeled rows for a fraud model. Your gradient booster hits 0.99 training AUC and 0.62 validation. Someone suggests adding the 200 more features 'we haven't tried yet.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the right move?
choices: Collect 10x more data before doing anything — the ratio is the only problem
Switch to a neural network — it handles high dimensions better
Add the 200 features — more signal can only help

Cut aggressively: with 400 features and 2k rows you are deep in curse-of-dimensionality territory (the model memorizes noise) — prune via L1 regularization or permutation importance, keep the top predictive subset, and validate the cut improves generalization
scenarios.why: The 0.99/0.62 gap with p≈n is textbook memorization: with 400 features the model finds spurious patterns in 2,000 rows. More features worsen it. The fix is reducing effective dimensionality — L1, importance-based pruning, or domain-guided selection — and confirming validation improves. More data would help eventually, but pruning is the immediate, controllable lever.
scenarios.hint: When features rival rows in count, what is the model actually learning?
objectives: Apply feature selection under p≈n conditions
evidence: Pruned a feature set and showed validation gain from the cut

scenarios.title: The Rolling Window That Saw Tomorrow
scenarios.situation: You build 'avg_spend_30d' as a rolling 30-day mean of daily spend per customer, computed over the full history table, then split into train/test by time. Validation looks great. In production the feature is computed from the live stream at scoring time — and performance drops.
scenarios.prompt: Where is the flaw in the time-based feature?
choices: The rolling window was computed over the full history without lagging: for a prediction made on date D, the window must cover only D-30..D-1 (strictly before the prediction moment) — an unlagged rolling mean at the boundary includes post-D data, leaking the future; recompute with a proper lag and verify point-in-time correctness
30 days is the wrong window — use 7 days
The time split is wrong — go back to a random split
Rolling means are bad features — use raw daily spend instead
scenarios.why: Rolling features are leakage-prone at the boundary: pandas rolling() centered on each row happily includes future rows unless explicitly shifted. At scoring time the future does not exist, so offline numbers were inflated. The fix is mechanical — lag/shift the window so every feature value uses only data knowable at prediction time — plus an audit that recomputes one customer by hand.
scenarios.hint: For a prediction stamped June 1, which dates may the 30-day window touch?
evidence: Rebuilt a rolling feature with a correct lag and verified it by hand

scenarios.title: Reading the Tickets
scenarios.situation: You have 80,000 support tickets with text and a 'will escalate' label. Your analyst instinct says the ticket text holds the signal. The team debates: fine-tune a large language model (3 weeks of work) or start with TF-IDF + logistic regression (one afternoon).
scenarios.prompt: What is the right sequencing?
choices: Fine-tune the LLM immediately — text means transformers, and starting simple wastes the afternoon

TF-IDF + logistic regression first: it is a strong, interpretable baseline for text classification that often reaches 80–90% of LLM performance in an afternoon — then decide if the remaining gap justifies 3 weeks of fine-tuning
Skip text entirely — text features are too noisy for production
Use word counts only — TF-IDF is overkill for a baseline
scenarios.why: TF-IDF + linear model is the honest baseline for text: fast, interpretable (top coefficients ARE the explanation), and surprisingly competitive. It also quantifies the prize — if the LLM only buys +2%, the 3 weeks are not worth it. Skipping the baseline means never knowing whether the complexity earned its keep.
scenarios.hint: What will you compare the 3-week model against if you never build the afternoon one?
evidence: Built a TF-IDF baseline and used it to scope further text-modeling work

scenarios.title: The Analyst's Ratio
scenarios.situation: Your churn model uses raw 'total_spend' and 'visit_count' features and plateaus. As an analyst you always looked at spend-PER-visit — a customer spending $500 across 2 visits behaves nothing like one spending $500 across 50 visits. The model cannot see that distinction in the raw columns.
scenarios.prompt: What feature-engineering move captures your analyst intuition?
choices: Drop one of the two columns — they are correlated
Add more raw columns — the model will discover the ratio itself

Engineer the interaction explicitly: spend_per_visit = total_spend / visit_count (plus trend ratios like recent_spend / prior_spend) — trees CAN approximate ratios with many splits, but handing them the ratio directly is far more sample-efficient, and it encodes domain knowledge the data alone may not reveal
Normalize both columns to 0–1 — the model will combine them
scenarios.why: Models learn what you feed them: a ratio the business thinks in should be a feature, not a hope. Trees approximate division only through deep, data-hungry split combinations; the explicit ratio gives the signal in one column. Your analyst ratios — per-visit, per-day, trend-vs-baseline — are feature engineering with domain priors, and they are why analysts often beat AutoML on business data.
scenarios.hint: If the business thinks in ratios, should the model have to rediscover them?
objectives: Encode analyst intuition as model inputs
evidence: Engineered a domain-ratio feature and measured its importance

domains.name: Model Evaluation That Matters
domains.description: Beyond accuracy: the metrics, validation schemes, and business framing that make models trustworthy.

scenarios.title: The Accurate Model Nobody Should Ship
scenarios.situation: Fraud model: 99.2% accuracy. The business pilot shows it catches 8% of fraud cases. The data scientist argues the accuracy proves it works.
scenarios.prompt: How do you respond?
choices: Agree — 99.2% accuracy is excellent; deploy it

Accuracy is meaningless at 1% fraud prevalence: the model predicts 'not fraud' almost always (99.2% = the base rate). Demand recall-focused evaluation: PR-AUC, recall at operational precision, and the business cost of missed fraud vs review workload
Collect more data — the model needs more examples
Tune the threshold to 0.99 to be safer
scenarios.why: 99.2% accuracy on 1%-fraud data is what 'predict never-fraud' achieves — the model may have learned literally nothing. The 8% recall is the truth: it misses 92% of fraud. The right response reframes evaluation around business cost: each missed fraud costs $X, each false alarm costs reviewer minutes. Choose the operating point (threshold) where marginal cost balances — and report PR-AUC, not accuracy, ever again on this data.
scenarios.hint: What does a constant 'not fraud' predictor score? What does the business actually pay for?
evidence: Model report
Accuracy 99.2%, ROC-AUC 0.81.
Pilot
Recall 8% at 0.5 threshold. Fraud prevalence 1%.

scenarios.title: The Threshold Nobody Set
scenarios.situation: Two churn models: Model A has higher AUC (0.88 vs 0.85), but at the business's operating threshold (top 10% riskiest get the retention offer), Model B catches 15% more actual churners. The team argues about which model is 'better.' The retention budget only covers 10% of customers.
scenarios.prompt: How do you resolve the disagreement?
choices: Average the two models' scores — ensembles beat arguments
Retrain both with more data and recompare AUC
Ship Model A — higher AUC is definitionally the better model

Evaluate at the operating point: AUC averages over all thresholds, but the business only operates at one — compare recall@10% (churners caught within the budgeted population); Model B wins where it counts, so the metric must match the decision, not the leaderboard
scenarios.why: AUC integrates performance across every threshold, including ones the business will never use. The decision is 'who gets the offer,' constrained to 10% — so recall@10% (or precision@k) is the metric that mirrors the decision. A model can have a better curve overall yet be worse exactly where you operate. Metrics must be chosen at the operating point.
scenarios.hint: The business does not operate at 'all thresholds' — where does it operate?
objectives: Evaluate models at the business operating point
Distinguish ranking metrics from decision metrics
evidence: Compared two models with a top-k metric tied to the budget constraint

scenarios.title: The Customer in Every Fold
scenarios.situation: Your dataset has 200,000 rows but only 20,000 customers (10 rows each — monthly snapshots). Standard 5-fold CV gives AUC 0.91. A colleague re-runs with GroupKFold grouped by customer and gets 0.78. The deployment will score NEW customers the model has never seen.
scenarios.prompt: Which CV result do you trust, and why?
choices: The 0.78: standard KFold leaks — the same customer appears in both train and validation folds, so the model memorizes customer identity instead of generalizing; GroupKFold (all of a customer's rows in one fold) reproduces the production condition of unseen customers
Average them — the truth is in the middle
Neither — use a single holdout instead
The 0.91 — more folds agreeing means a more reliable estimate
scenarios.why: Rows from the same customer are not independent: with 10 rows per customer scattered across folds, the model learns 'this customer churns' rather than general churn patterns — a form of leakage through the split. GroupKFold keeps each customer's rows together, matching deployment on new customers. The 0.13 gap is the memorization premium, not real performance.
scenarios.hint: In production, will the model ever see a customer it trained on?
evidence: Re-ran CV with grouping and explained the score drop

scenarios.title: The Test Set That Flattered Everyone
scenarios.situation: Your holdout test set was sampled from the same cleaned, deduplicated warehouse table as training. In production, the model scores raw event-stream data with duplicates, missing fields, and timezone inconsistencies. Pilot performance is far below the test estimate, and every model you tried showed the same gap.
scenarios.prompt: What went wrong in test-set construction?
choices: The test set was too small — sampling noise explains the gap

The test set does not represent the production distribution: it was drawn from cleaned warehouse data, but the model serves messy stream data — the test set must mirror the serving-time input distribution, warts included, or the estimate is fiction
You need cross-validation instead of a holdout — holdouts are unreliable
The models are all underfit — the gap is a modeling problem
scenarios.why: A test set is a contract: 'performance on this approximates performance in production.' Sampling it from a cleaner distribution than serving voids the contract for every model equally — which is why all models showed the same gap. The fix is constructing the test set from production-like inputs (raw stream samples, labeled after the fact), not from the training warehouse.
scenarios.hint: What data does the model actually see when it serves — and is that what the test set contains?
evidence: Rebuilt a test set from production-distribution samples

scenarios.title: Slicing the Errors
scenarios.situation: Overall churn-model precision is 0.72 — acceptable. But error analysis by segment shows: enterprise customers 0.91 precision, SMB 0.68, and startup-plan customers 0.31 — the model is nearly useless for startups, who are 25% of the base. The aggregate metric hid the failure.
scenarios.prompt: What is the right response?
choices: Lower the threshold for startups only — a quick calibration tweak
Ship it — 0.72 overall meets the bar; segments are noise

Do sliced error analysis and act on it: the startup segment needs diagnosis (different behavior? too few examples? missing features like funding-stage?) — then target the fix (segment-specific features, more startup data, or a separate model) and add segment metrics to the evaluation gate
Remove startup customers from the data — the model is for the other segments
scenarios.why: Aggregate metrics are averages that hide segment failures — and the failing segment is a quarter of the business. Sliced evaluation turns 'the model works' into 'the model works for whom.' The fix starts with diagnosis (representation? features? behavior shift?) because the remedy differs: more data vs better features vs a separate model. Segment metrics then become permanent quality gates.
scenarios.hint: Who is the 0.72 actually describing — and who is it hiding?
objectives: Convert segment failures into targeted fixes
evidence: Ran segment-sliced evaluation and proposed a segment-specific fix

scenarios.title: The One-Seed Shootout
scenarios.situation: A teammate claims their tuned XGBoost (AUC 0.843) beats your random forest (AUC 0.839) and wants to ship it. Both numbers come from a single train/test split with one random seed. You re-run both with five different seeds: XGBoost ranges 0.831–0.849, forest ranges 0.834–0.844.
scenarios.prompt: How do you compare the models rigorously?
choices: Run 100 seeds and pick the best one for each model, then compare bests
Average the ranges and ship whichever average is higher regardless of overlap
Ship the XGBoost — 0.843 > 0.839, the numbers speak

The 0.004 gap is noise: compare on the SAME folds/seeds (paired comparison), look at the range overlap, and require the difference to exceed seed variance — here the ranges fully overlap, so there is no evidence of a real difference; pick on other grounds (speed, simplicity, interpretability)
scenarios.why: Single-seed comparisons confuse luck with superiority: the seed ranges overlap completely, so the 'win' is sampling noise. Rigorous comparison fixes the randomness (same seeds/folds for both — paired), then asks whether the difference survives the variance. When it does not, the tie-breakers are engineering virtues, not the fourth decimal of AUC.
scenarios.hint: If you re-ran the 'winning' model with a new seed, would it still win?
objectives: Distinguish real gains from seed noise
evidence: Compared two models with paired seeds and a variance-aware verdict

scenarios.title: Confident and Wrong
scenarios.situation: Your churn model's predicted probabilities feed a budget allocator: expected churners × offer cost. The model ranks well (AUC 0.87), but calibration plots show: when it says 80% churn risk, only 50% actually churn. Finance's budget forecasts are systematically overshooting.
scenarios.prompt: What evaluation step was missed, and what is the fix?
choices: Calibration was never checked: ranking (AUC) and probability quality are different properties — plot predicted vs observed rates, then fix with calibration (Platt scaling / isotonic regression on a held-out set) or use a model whose probabilities are natively better calibrated
The threshold is wrong — recalibrate the 0.5 cutoff
Finance should not use model outputs — probabilities are inherently unreliable
AUC is wrong — switch to accuracy for budget decisions
scenarios.why: AUC measures ranking — 'higher-risk customers score above lower-risk ones' — but says nothing about whether 0.8 means 80%. Budget math needs calibrated probabilities (0.8 ≈ 80% actual). Gradient boosters are notoriously miscalibrated (overconfident). The fix is a separate calibration step on held-out data, verified with reliability diagrams — a different evaluation axis than discrimination.
scenarios.hint: AUC answers 'is A riskier than B?' — but finance asked a different question. What was it?
objectives: Apply probability calibration for decision use
evidence: Checked a calibration plot and applied a calibration fix

scenarios.title: Offline Up, Business Flat
scenarios.situation: Model v2 beats v1 offline on every metric: AUC +0.03, log-loss down, precision up at all thresholds. The A/B test runs for a month: retention-offer acceptance is identical between v1 and v2 arms. Product declares ML 'not working.'
scenarios.prompt: How do you diagnose the offline-online gap?
choices: The offline metrics are lying — stop trusting them entirely

Check the causal chain: offline metrics measure prediction quality, but the business metric measures prediction → action → outcome — audit whether v2's 'better' predictions actually changed WHO got offers (maybe the same customers), whether the offer itself works, and whether the test had power; a better ranker cannot move a metric if the intervention is ineffective or the top-k population barely changed
v2 overfit — the offline gains are fake
Run the A/B test longer — a month is never enough
scenarios.why: Offline metrics evaluate the model; business metrics evaluate the model PLUS the intervention PLUS the targeting overlap. If v2 ranks the same top customers as v1, or the retention offer itself does not change behavior, no prediction improvement can move the business number. The diagnosis walks the chain: did the scored population change? did actions change? did outcomes respond to actions? Blaming the model skips two links.
scenarios.hint: Between the prediction and the revenue, what has to happen — and did v2 change any of it?
evidence: Audited the action chain behind a flat A/B test on an improved model

domains.name: From Notebook to Production
domains.description: What changes when a model meets reality: pipelines, monitoring, drift, and the MLOps minimum.

scenarios.title: The Model That Quietly Died
scenarios.situation: The lead-scoring model worked for 8 months. Conversions from 'hot' leads have decayed 30% over the last quarter. No errors in the pipeline; features are all populated.
scenarios.prompt: What is the diagnosis path?
choices: Retrain immediately on recent data — fresher is better

Drift investigation: compare feature distributions now vs training (input drift), check prediction distribution shift, verify label definition hasn't changed, audit for upstream pipeline changes — then decide whether retraining, feature fixes, or problem reframing is warranted
The sales team stopped following up — it's a people problem
Add more features — the model needs more signal
scenarios.why: Silent decay with healthy pipelines is drift until proven otherwise — but WHICH drift decides the fix. Input drift (feature distributions moved) → retrain or fix features. Label drift (what counts as 'converted' changed) → reframe. Upstream change (a form field renamed) → pipeline fix. Blind retraining on drifted data can bake in the problem. The diagnosis order: distributions, labels, upstream — then act. And this is why the MLOps minimum includes drift monitors: this should have paged at 10%, not been discovered at 30%.
scenarios.hint: No errors, full features, decaying outcomes. What moves silently? What should have paged earlier?
evidence: Business metric
'Hot' lead conversion: 22% → 15% over 13 weeks.
Pipeline
All jobs green. Feature null rates unchanged.

scenarios.title: Batch or Real-Time?
scenarios.situation: The churn model will drive a monthly retention email campaign. An engineer proposes a real-time scoring API 'for freshness'; it needs 99.9% uptime, sub-200ms latency, on-call rotation, and 6 weeks of infra work. The campaign list is generated once a month from the warehouse.
scenarios.prompt: Which deployment pattern fits, and why?
choices: Real-time, but only for high-value customers — a hybrid
Real-time API — fresher scores are always better, and the infra work is a good investment

Batch scoring: the decision cadence is monthly and the data lives in the warehouse — a scheduled batch job that scores all customers and writes results to a table meets the need with a fraction of the complexity, cost, and operational burden
Both — build the API now for future use cases
scenarios.why: Deployment pattern follows decision cadence: monthly campaign → monthly batch. A real-time API buys nothing here — scores would sit unused for 29 days — while adding latency SLOs, uptime burden, and 6 weeks of work. The simplest system that meets the decision's freshness requirement wins; complexity is a cost, not a feature.
scenarios.hint: How often is the score actually USED — and what does freshness buy in between?
objectives: Match deployment pattern to decision cadence
Weigh operational cost of serving choices
evidence: Chose batch vs real-time serving from the decision cadence

scenarios.title: Flying Blind on Labels
scenarios.situation: Your churn model predicts 90-day churn, so true labels arrive 90 days late. Last quarter the model's decisions quietly degraded — nobody noticed for two months because 'accuracy dashboards' had no fresh labels to compute. The business wants a monitoring design that catches the next decay in days, not months.
scenarios.prompt: What do you monitor when labels are delayed?
choices: Retrain weekly — fresh models do not need monitoring
Monitor only the business metric (retention rate) — it is the only thing that matters
Nothing until labels arrive — without ground truth, monitoring is impossible

Monitor what IS observable now: input feature distributions (drift detection on top features), prediction distribution shifts (is the score histogram moving?), data quality (null rates, schema changes, volume anomalies), and upstream pipeline health — plus a small fast-label sample (e.g., early churn signals) as a leading indicator
scenarios.why: Label delay does not mean blindness: feature drift, prediction drift, and data-quality signals are all computable immediately and usually precede performance decay. A model can break (upstream schema change, broken feature) weeks before labels confirm it. The monitoring design layers fast proxies (distributions, nulls, volumes) under slow truth (labels), with alerting thresholds on each.
scenarios.hint: Labels are late, but what about the INPUTS and the OUTPUTS — are they late too?
objectives: Layer fast proxies beneath slow ground truth
evidence: Specified a monitoring plan with drift, distribution, and quality signals

scenarios.title: The Retraining Calendar
scenarios.situation: Team policy: retrain the demand-forecast model on the 1st of every month, no exceptions. In March, a supply-chain shock shifts buying patterns mid-month; the model serves stale patterns for six weeks. In quiet months, retraining changes nothing but burns compute and risks regressions.
scenarios.prompt: What retraining policy replaces the fixed calendar?
choices: Trigger-based retraining: monitor feature drift, prediction drift, and the business metric; retrain when drift exceeds thresholds or performance decays — with the monthly schedule as a backstop, not the driver; every retrain still passes the shadow/champion-challenger gate before promotion
Never retrain — the original model was validated once
Retrain only when someone complains — human-triggered is cheapest
Retrain daily — fresher is always better
scenarios.why: Fixed schedules retrain when nothing changed (waste + regression risk) and miss real shifts between dates (the March shock). Triggers tie retraining to evidence: drift metrics and business KPIs say WHEN, the pipeline says HOW. The schedule remains as a maximum-staleness backstop. And triggers do not bypass validation — every candidate still earns promotion.
scenarios.hint: What should cause a retrain — the calendar, or evidence that the world changed?
objectives: Combine drift triggers with scheduled backstops
evidence: Defined retraining triggers with thresholds and a backstop schedule

scenarios.title: Which v2 Is in Production?
scenarios.situation: Production serves 'churn_model_v2.pkl' — but there are three files with that name from different months, trained on different data snapshots, with different hyperparameters. A bug report comes in and nobody can say which model is actually serving, what data trained it, or how to rebuild it.
scenarios.prompt: What does proper model versioning require?
choices: Better filenames — v2_final_FINAL.pkl conventions work if the team is disciplined

A model registry entry per version: immutable artifact + training data version/hash + code commit + hyperparameters + metrics + training timestamp + promotion status (staging/production/archived) — 'v2' becomes a pointer to one specific, rebuildable lineage, not a filename
One model file, overwritten in place — then there is only ever one version
Version the code only — the model follows the code
scenarios.why: A model version is not a file — it is the full lineage (data, code, config, metrics) that produced the artifact. Filenames are not immutable and carry no lineage; overwriting destroys history; code-only versioning ignores data and hyperparameters, which change outcomes as much as code. The registry makes 'what is serving' an answerable, auditable question.
scenarios.hint: If you had to rebuild EXACTLY this model in a year, what would you need — and where is it written down?
evidence: Specified the lineage fields of a model registry entry

scenarios.title: The Rollback That Wasn't There
scenarios.situation: Churn model v3 deploys Friday at 5pm. By Monday, the retention team reports the offer list looks wrong — v3 scores every enterprise account near zero. Rolling back means: find the old artifact (hopefully), rebuild the serving config by hand, redeploy, and pray. It takes 11 hours.
scenarios.prompt: What rollback design prevents this?
choices: Roll forward with a v3.1 hotfix — always fix forward
Never deploy on Fridays — the process fix is cultural

Design rollback BEFORE deployment: keep the previous version warm (blue/green or a config flag pointing at model versions), version the serving config alongside the model, and rehearse the rollback — recovery should be a flag flip in minutes, not an 11-hour rebuild
Test more before deploying — rollback is for teams that do not test
scenarios.why: Rollback is a design property, not a hope: blue/green (or version-flagged) serving keeps v2 one switch away, and versioned configs make the switch deterministic. 'Don't deploy Friday' reduces blast radius timing but leaves the 11-hour recovery intact. Fix-forward is fine when the fix is known; when the failure is mysterious at 9am Monday, you need the instant, boring, rehearsed path back.
scenarios.hint: At the moment of failure, what is the SINGLE action that restores service — and does it exist yet?
objectives: Design instant rollback for model deployments
Version serving config with the model
evidence: Sketched a blue/green model deployment with a flag-flip rollback

scenarios.title: The Shadow Knows
scenarios.situation: Model v4 beats v3 offline by a solid margin. The team is split: half want to ship to 100% immediately ('the metrics are clear'), half want a month-long A/B test ('production is different'). Meanwhile v4 has never seen a single real production request.
scenarios.prompt: What deployment sequence resolves this safely?
choices: A/B test for a month immediately — skip shadow, it delays learning
Keep v3 — if the team disagrees, the safe choice is no change
Ship to 100% — offline metrics were clear and A/B tests are slow

Shadow mode first: run v4 alongside v3 on live traffic, log its predictions without acting on them, and compare against actuals and v3 — then canary to a small traffic slice with rollback ready, then full rollout; each stage buys evidence the previous stage could not
scenarios.why: Shadow deployment is the missing evidence stage: it exposes v4 to real production inputs (distribution, edge cases, latency) with zero user impact, catching training-serving skew before any customer sees it. Canary then limits blast radius while measuring business impact. Jumping to 100% gambles the whole business on offline metrics; month-long A/B without shadow wastes weeks discovering what shadow shows in days.
scenarios.hint: What is the cheapest way to let v4 meet reality without letting reality meet v4?
objectives: Match deployment stages to evidence needs
evidence: Designed a staged rollout with evidence gates at each stage

scenarios.title: The Nulls That Nobody Saw
scenarios.situation: An upstream warehouse migration silently changes 'last_login_days_ago' from integer days to a string column with 'unknown' for missing values. Your feature pipeline coerces it, fills nothing, and the model starts scoring 'unknown' customers with garbage features. No alert fires for three weeks — the pipeline 'succeeded' every night.
scenarios.prompt: What pipeline design catches this on night one?
choices: Data validation gates in the pipeline: schema checks (column names, types), distribution checks (null rate, value ranges vs a reference window), and volume checks — failing the nightly job LOUDLY on violation instead of silently coercing; the pipeline should refuse to produce features it cannot vouch for
A bigger model — robust models tolerate bad inputs
Manual QA of the warehouse every morning — human eyes catch what code misses
More unit tests on the model code — the model is the important part
scenarios.why: Silent coercion is the failure: the pipeline succeeded while producing garbage, because nothing asserted what 'good input' looks like. Validation gates (schema, null-rate, range, volume vs reference) turn upstream breakage into a failed job with an alert on night one — failing loudly beats serving silently-wrong scores. Model robustness and manual QA are complements, not substitutes, for input contracts.
scenarios.hint: The pipeline 'succeeded.' What should 'success' have required it to prove?
objectives: Design data validation gates for feature pipelines
Prefer loud failure over silent corruption
evidence: Wrote input-contract checks (schema, nulls, ranges) for a feature pipeline

scenarios.title: The Shape Mismatch
scenarios.situation: Your sklearn Pipeline (OneHotEncoder + StandardScaler in a ColumnTransformer, then LogisticRegression) throws: 'ValueError: X has 47 features, but LogisticRegression is expecting 52 features as input.' It worked last week. The only change: the input CSV gained a new product category value.
scenarios.prompt: What broke, and what is the robust fix?
choices: LogisticRegression is buggy with pipelines — train it outside the pipeline

OneHotEncoder learned 52 columns at fit time; the new category at transform time changes the encoded width (or handle_unknown drops/mismatches it) — the robust fix is handle_unknown='ignore' (stable width) PLUS a data-validation gate that alerts on unseen categories instead of silently changing feature space
The CSV is corrupt — revert to last week's file
Add 5 dummy columns to force 52 features — match the expected width
scenarios.why: One-hot width is fit-time state: new categories at transform time break the contract (or silently alter it, depending on handle_unknown). handle_unknown='ignore' keeps the width stable, but silently ignoring is its own risk — hence the validation gate that pages someone when the category set drifts. The error is the pipeline telling the truth; the fix makes the truth boring.
scenarios.hint: Where does the number 52 come from — and what could change it at 2am?
evidence: Fixed a pipeline shape error and added a category-drift gate

scenarios.title: The Warning That Meant Underfit
scenarios.situation: Your LogisticRegression training prints ConvergenceWarning: 'lbfgs failed to converge (status=1): increase max_iter or scale the data.' The model still returns scores, so you ship the numbers into the evaluation. AUC is 0.68 — well below the 0.80 your colleague got on the same data.
scenarios.prompt: What does the warning mean, and what is the fix?
choices: The data has no signal — 0.68 is all there is
Nothing — the model returned scores, so it worked; the 0.68 is the true performance

The optimizer quit before finding the solution: unscaled features (revenue in millions vs rates in decimals) make the loss surface ill-conditioned, so lbfgs stalls at max_iter — fix by scaling features (StandardScaler in the Pipeline) and/or raising max_iter; the 0.68 measures an unconverged model, not the data's signal
Switch to a different solver randomly until the warning disappears
scenarios.why: ConvergenceWarning means the optimizer stopped early — the coefficients are not the solution, they're where the algorithm gave up. Unscaled features are the usual cause (the loss landscape becomes a narrow valley lbfgs can't navigate in 100 iterations). Scaling fixes the geometry; max_iter buys more steps. Evaluating an unconverged model measures optimizer failure, not model quality.
scenarios.hint: If the optimizer 'failed to converge,' what exactly are those coefficients?
evidence: Resolved a ConvergenceWarning and recovered the expected score

scenarios.title: Works on My Machine
scenarios.situation: Your model trains fine on your laptop (scikit-learn 1.3) but crashes on the training server (scikit-learn 1.1): 'HistGradientBoostingClassifier got an unexpected keyword argument.' The server is managed by another team and 'upgrading is scheduled for next quarter.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the durable fix?
choices: Train on the server via SSH — develop where you deploy
Vendor the sklearn source into your repo — total control
Rewrite the model to avoid the new parameter — code to the lowest common denominator

Pin the environment as code: a requirements.txt / lockfile (or container) declaring exact versions, built identically on laptop and server — 'works on my machine' is an environment bug, and the fix is making environments reproducible, not dumbing down the code (with a fallback shim only if the server truly cannot be aligned)
scenarios.why: Version drift between dev and prod is an environment-reproducibility failure, and the durable fix is declarative environments (lockfiles/containers) — the same bytes everywhere. Coding to the oldest version works once but ratchets the whole team down to the slowest upgrade cycle. SSH-dev fixes your machine, not the team's.
scenarios.hint: Is the bug in your code, or in the assumption that two machines are the same?
evidence: Wrote a lockfile that reproduces an ML environment on two machines

scenarios.title: The Silent dtype Change
scenarios.situation: After an upstream CSV export change, your 'is_premium' column arrives as strings ('True'/'False') instead of booleans. pandas reads it as object dtype. Your pipeline's SimpleImputer(strategy='mean') now crashes — but only on the full nightly run; your local sample (old file) still works.
scenarios.prompt: What two defenses does this incident demand?
choices: Defense 1: schema validation at ingestion (assert expected dtypes/values before the pipeline runs, fail loudly on violation). Defense 2: make the pipeline robust by declaring dtypes explicitly (converters/dtype specs) rather than inferring them — inference is a guess that upstream changes break silently
Switch to a different imputation strategy that handles strings
Email the upstream team and wait — their bug, their fix
Cast the column manually in the notebook and move on — one-line fix
scenarios.why: Two failures compounded: the pipeline inferred dtypes (a guess), and nothing validated the guess at ingestion (no alarm). Explicit dtype declarations remove the guess; ingestion-time schema checks convert silent corruption into a loud, fast failure. The manual cast fixes today's file; the two defenses fix the class of incident.
scenarios.hint: Why did it work locally and fail nightly — what differed between the two inputs?
objectives: Declare dtypes explicitly instead of inferring
evidence: Added ingestion schema checks that fail loudly on dtype changes

scenarios.title: The Nondeterministic Notebook
scenarios.situation: Your experiment notebook produces a different validation score every run: 0.81, 0.84, 0.79, 0.83. You set random_state=42 on the model. The data loader shuffles with numpy's global RNG (unseeded), and train_test_split has no random_state. Your experiment log is now meaningless — which run was 'the' result?
scenarios.prompt: What is the complete reproducibility fix?
choices: Set random_state=42 in more places until the numbers stabilize

Seed EVERYTHING deterministically: a single master seed fanning out to each component (split, shuffle, model, CV), set PYTHONHASHSEED, pin library versions, and log the seed + versions with each run — one unseeded RNG anywhere reintroduces the chaos, so the fix is systematic, not incremental
Average 20 runs and report the mean — noise averages out
Accept nondeterminism — real science embraces variance
scenarios.why: Reproducibility is all-or-nothing: a single unseeded RNG (the loader's shuffle here) poisons the whole run, which is why seeding 'the model' wasn't enough. The systematic fix covers every randomness source plus the environment (versions, hash seed), with the seed logged per run. Averaging hides the problem; embracing it makes experiments unrepeatable.
scenarios.hint: You seeded the model. What ELSE in the notebook rolls dice?
objectives: Enumerate all randomness sources in an ML script
evidence: Made a notebook bit-reproducible across runs

scenarios.title: The 40GB CSV
scenarios.situation: Your feature-engineering script does pd.read_csv('events.csv') on a 40GB file. The process gets OOM-killed at 92% every time. You actually need only 6 of 80 columns, one month of dates, and per-user aggregates — but 'just load it and filter' keeps dying.
scenarios.prompt: What is the memory-efficient approach?
choices: Convert to Excel first — Excel handles big files better
Get a bigger machine with 128GB RAM — hardware solves it

Push the filtering down: read only needed columns (usecols), parse dates once with explicit dtypes (downcast ints/floats, category for low-cardinality strings), filter rows in chunks (chunksize) aggregating incrementally — never materialize the full 40GB; the 6-column, 1-month, aggregated result fits in memory easily
Sample 1% of rows — close enough for features
scenarios.why: The OOM is self-inflicted: loading 80 columns to use 6, full-precision dtypes, and the whole file at once. Column pruning + dtype downcasting often cuts 5–10x; chunked incremental aggregation means memory stays flat regardless of file size. Sampling changes the aggregates' correctness; bigger hardware just postpones the same mistake to the next file size.
scenarios.hint: What fraction of the 40GB do you actually NEED — and when must it be in memory?
objectives: Reduce pandas memory with dtypes and column pruning
evidence: Processed a file larger than RAM with chunked aggregation

scenarios.title: Fit on the Future
scenarios.situation: A teammate's code: scaler.fit_transform(X) on the FULL dataset, then train_test_split. Validation AUC is 0.93 — spectacular. You rerun with the scaler fit on train only: 0.84. The teammate says '0.93 is the real number, your version just has less data for the scaler.'
scenarios.prompt: Who is right, and what is the code fix?
choices: Both are valid — report the average, 0.885
Scaling is the problem — drop the scaler entirely
The teammate — more data for the scaler means better normalization

You are: fitting the scaler on full data leaks test-set statistics (means/variances) into training — the 0.93 is contaminated; the fix is fit-on-train-only, best enforced structurally with a Pipeline (scaler inside the pipeline, fit only on train folds) so the mistake becomes impossible, not just discouraged
scenarios.why: Preprocessing fit on full data is leakage through statistics: test means/variances inform the training transform, inflating validation. The 0.09 gap is the contamination premium. The durable fix is structural — sklearn Pipeline fits transformers on train folds only, making the correct order the only order. 'More data for the scaler' misunderstands what the scaler is allowed to see.
scenarios.hint: What does the scaler LEARN — and from whom is it allowed to learn it?
evidence: Refactored leaky preprocessing into a Pipeline and measured the honest score

scenarios.title: The 6-Hour Grid Search
scenarios.situation: Your GridSearchCV over 200 hyperparameter combos takes 6 hours. Each iteration of your feature work means another 6 hours. You are iterating once a day and the project is stalling — but you're afraid to shrink the search because 'thoroughness.'
scenarios.prompt: How do you get iteration speed back without losing rigor?
choices: Shrink the iteration loop, not the rigor: develop on a stratified 10–20% data sample with a coarse randomized search (fast signal on what matters), then run the full search ONCE on the shortlist before final evaluation — plus n_jobs=-1, early stopping where supported, and caching preprocessed features so the search doesn't recompute them 200 times
Tune on the test set — it's faster than CV
Pick hyperparameters randomly once and never tune again
Keep the 6-hour search — rigor requires patience
scenarios.why: Iteration speed IS rigor: a practitioner who tests 10 ideas a day with coarse search learns more than one who tests 1 idea with exhaustive search. The two-stage pattern (fast coarse signal on a sample → one full run on finalists) preserves decision quality while collapsing the loop. Caching and parallelism attack the constant factors. Tuning on test corrupts the final estimate — speed never justifies that.
scenarios.hint: What are you actually trying to LEARN from the search — and how cheaply can you learn it?
objectives: Optimize iteration speed in ML development
evidence: Cut a tuning loop from hours to minutes with sampling + coarse search

domains.description: The Python you need for ML: pandas fluency, sklearn basics, and the notebook discipline.

domains.name: Statistics Refresh
domains.description: The stats that matter for ML: distributions, inference, and the intuition behind the math.

domains.name: ML Project Playbook
domains.description: Run an ML project end-to-end: scoping, baselines, iteration, and the demo.

scenarios.title: From 'Use ML' to a Real Problem
scenarios.situation: Leadership's brief: 'Use ML to reduce churn.' No target metric, no defined action, no owner of the decision the model would inform. Two analysts already spent a month 'exploring' with nothing to show. You are asked to take over and 'make the ML happen.'
scenarios.prompt: What is the correct scoping move?
choices: Refuse the project — vague briefs always fail

Convert the vague brief into a decidable prediction task: WHO decides WHAT, WHEN, with WHAT action available — e.g., 'predict 30-day churn risk to prioritize the monthly retention call list, success = +5pts offer-acceptance vs control' — and get the decision owner to sign off before any modeling
Build a churn dashboard first — descriptive work always helps
Start modeling immediately — exploration will reveal the problem
scenarios.why: ML projects die in vagueness: without a decision, an action, and a success metric, no model can succeed because success is undefined. The scoping move translates 'use ML' into prediction → decision → action → metric, with a named owner. This takes days and prevents months of aimless exploration. A dashboard is fine work, but it answers a different brief.
scenarios.hint: What decision will the model's output change — and who owns that decision?
objectives: Scope vague ML briefs into decidable tasks
evidence: Wrote a one-page ML project scope with decision, action, and metric

scenarios.title: The 99% Promise
scenarios.situation: In the kickoff, the VP says: 'So we'll get 99% accuracy, right? That's what AI does now.' The room nods. You know the base rate is 88% (predict-nothing territory) and a realistic target is 93–94% with real business value. Correcting the VP publicly feels risky; staying silent feels worse.
scenarios.prompt: How do you manage this expectation?
choices: Stay silent — contradicting the VP kills the project politically
Promise 99% — aim high and figure it out later

Reframe on the spot with the baseline: 'Predicting nothing scores 88%, so the question is what we gain above 88 — our target is X with $Y business value, and I'll report progress against that baseline weekly' — replace the fantasy number with the honest frame plus a business metric, in the meeting, respectfully
Send a technical memo after the meeting explaining why 99% is impossible
scenarios.why: Uncorrected fantasy numbers become the project's success criteria, guaranteeing perceived failure. The reframe works because it does not say 'you're wrong' — it installs a better yardstick (baseline + business value) that makes 93% a win instead of 99% a failure. Done live, it prevents the number from hardening; a memo after the fact fights an entrenched expectation.
scenarios.hint: What happens to the project if 99% becomes the official target?
evidence: Reframed an accuracy demand into a baseline-plus-value target

scenarios.title: The Smallest Useful Model
scenarios.situation: The churn project has a 12-week runway. The proposed plan: weeks 1–10 building the 'real' model (feature store, deep learning, real-time API), weeks 11–12 'deployment.' You have seen this movie — month three arrives with nothing shippable and the sponsor asks what the team did all quarter.
scenarios.prompt: How do you define the MVP?
choices: A slide deck describing the future model — align stakeholders first
The feature store — infrastructure first, modeling second
The full plan is the MVP — cutting scope cuts quality

The MVP is the smallest thing that delivers a real decision: batch-scored logistic regression on 10 solid features, written to a table the retention team already uses, in week 3 — it proves the full loop (data → model → action → measured outcome) and every later upgrade is optional, not existential
scenarios.why: The MVP's job is de-risking the loop, not maximizing the model: a simple model in production in week 3 surfaces every real problem (data gaps, action friction, measurement) while there is still time to fix them. The 12-week big-bang plan discovers those problems in week 11. Infrastructure and sophistication are week-4+ upgrades to a working loop, not prerequisites.
scenarios.hint: What is the riskiest unknown — the model math, or everything around it?
objectives: Define ML MVPs around the decision loop
evidence: Scoped an ML MVP that ships the full loop in weeks, not quarters

scenarios.title: The Honest Estimate
scenarios.situation: You are asked: 'How long to production?' Your gut says 6 weeks of modeling. Experience says: data access (2 weeks of tickets), label definition fights (1 week), feature pipeline (2 weeks), stakeholder reviews (1 week), deployment (2 weeks). The sponsor wants '6 weeks' on the slide.
scenarios.prompt: How do you estimate?
choices: Estimate the full system, not the model: present the 10–12 week breakdown with the non-modeling work itemized (data, labels, pipeline, reviews, deploy) — because in ML projects the model is ~20% of the work, and hiding the 80% guarantees a missed date
Say 16 weeks with padding — under-promise, over-deliver
Refuse to estimate — ML is research, not engineering
Say 6 weeks — sponsors want confidence, and you can compress the rest
scenarios.why: ML timelines blow up in the non-modeling work, which is also the work sponsors forget exists. Itemizing it makes the estimate credible AND educates the sponsor on where time goes — turning 'why so long?' into a shared plan. Blind padding without breakdown looks evasive; '6 weeks' is a date you will miss in week 4 when the data ticket is still open.
scenarios.hint: Where did your last three ML projects actually spend their weeks?
objectives: Make non-modeling work visible in plans
evidence: Produced an itemized ML timeline with non-modeling work called out

scenarios.title: The Pilot That Flopped
scenarios.situation: The churn pilot ran 6 weeks: the model scored well offline, but offer-acceptance in the treatment group matched control. The sponsor calls it a failure and wants the plug pulled. You have one meeting to respond. The data shows the treatment group DID get different (higher-risk) customers — the offer just did not move them.
scenarios.prompt: How do you handle the failure?
choices: Agree it failed and shut it down — the metric is the metric

Run a blameless postmortem that separates the layers: the MODEL worked (better targeting), the INTERVENTION didn't (the offer doesn't change behavior) — then propose the pivot the evidence supports: test stronger interventions on the model's ranked list, because the targeting asset is proven even though this offer flopped
Blame the data — the pilot was underpowered
Tune the model and rerun the same pilot — the model must be the problem
scenarios.why: Collapsing 'model' and 'intervention' into one verdict wastes a proven asset: the pilot proved targeting works and the offer does not — two separate facts with separate remedies. The postmortem's job is layered attribution (data → model → action → outcome), which converts 'failure' into 'we built a good ranker; now we need an offer worth ranking for.' Retuning the model fixes the layer that wasn't broken.
scenarios.hint: Which layer actually failed — the ranking, or what was done with the ranking?
objectives: Attribute ML pilot failures by layer
Pivot from failed pilots using evidence
evidence: Wrote a layered postmortem separating model, action, and outcome

scenarios.title: What Counts as Churn?
scenarios.situation: Marketing defines churn as 'no login in 30 days.' Finance defines it as 'canceled subscription.' Support defines it as 'account closed.' Your model needs ONE label. Each team insists theirs is 'the real churn,' and the label choice changes the target population by 40%.
scenarios.prompt: How do you adjudicate the label definition?
choices: Pick marketing's — they are the stakeholder
Average the three definitions into a composite label

Tie the label to the decision: the model drives retention OFFERS, which only make sense for customers who can still be saved — so the label is 'will cancel in the next 30 days while still active,' the definition the ACTION requires; document the choice, show each team how their definition maps to it, and get sign-off
Build three models, one per definition — let the best win
scenarios.why: Labels are not found, they are chosen — and the right chooser is the downstream action. Retention offers target saveable customers, so 'canceled subscription within 30d' (finance's, roughly) fits the action; 'no login' includes dormant-but-paying customers the offer cannot help. Three models triple the maintenance for a definitional dispute. Decide by action-fit, document, align.
scenarios.hint: Who ACTS on the prediction — and which definition makes their action sensible?
objectives: Derive label definitions from downstream actions
evidence: Documented a label definition tied to the consuming decision

scenarios.title: The Bar Before the Build
scenarios.situation: The team is excited: embeddings, a feature store, real-time serving. Nobody has written down what 'success' means. You ask: 'What number, on what metric, makes this worth what we're spending?' Silence. Then: 'We'll know it when we see it.'
scenarios.prompt: What success criteria do you lock in before building?
choices: AUC > 0.9 — a clear technical bar is enough
Beat the competitor's published numbers — external benchmarks motivate
None — prespecifying metrics constrains creativity

A written contract: the business metric (e.g., incremental retained revenue), the minimum meaningful lift (worth the build+run cost), the offline proxy that predicts it, and the decision rule ('ship if pilot shows +X with Y confidence; kill if not by week Z') — signed off before modeling starts
scenarios.why: 'We'll know it when we see it' is how projects drift forever: every result gets reinterpreted as success. The contract separates the business metric (money) from the offline proxy (AUC) and pre-commits the ship/kill rule — which also protects the team from moving goalposts. A technical bar alone (AUC 0.9) can be met while the business metric never moves.
scenarios.hint: If the pilot shows +2% with wide error bars, is that a ship or a kill — and who decided?
objectives: Separate business metrics from offline proxies
evidence: Wrote a ship/kill contract with business metric, bar, and decision rule

scenarios.title: The Handoff Package
scenarios.situation: Your churn model works in the notebook. The platform team, who will productionize it, asks for 'the handoff.' You send the notebook. They return it with 40 comments: no pinned dependencies, features computed with notebook-only SQL, no input schema, no idea what 'good' looks like in production, no rollback plan.
scenarios.prompt: What belongs in a production handoff package?
